nameStory: Coccotylus truncatus gets its scientific name from Latin words meaning "berry-like leaf" and "cut off abruptly," referring to its flattened, somewhat rounded fronds that often appear to end suddenly rather than tapering to a point. This red seaweed doesn't have a widely-used common name, so marine biologists and seaweed enthusiasts usually just call it by its scientific name.
description: Coccotylus truncatus is a red seaweed (marine algae) that grows attached to rocks in cold ocean waters. It forms flattened, leathery fronds that are deep red to purplish-red in color and can grow up to 6 inches tall. The fronds are relatively thick and sturdy compared to many other seaweeds, with a somewhat rubbery texture. Unlike land plants, this marine algae doesn't have true leaves, stems, or roots, but instead has a simple body called a thallus.

idTips.label: Truncated frond tips
idTips.description: The fronds end abruptly as if cut with scissors, rather than tapering to a point - this blunt, squared-off appearance is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Thick, leathery texture
idTips.description: Fronds feel substantial and rubbery when touched, much thicker than tissue paper-thin seaweeds, with a texture similar to a thick rubber glove

idTips.label: Deep red coloration
idTips.description: Rich burgundy to deep purplish-red color that remains vibrant even when wet, though may appear darker or almost black when submerged

idTips.label: Flattened fronds
idTips.description: Fronds are distinctly flattened like ribbons rather than cylindrical, typically 1-3 inches wide and lying relatively flat against rocks

idTips.label: Rock attachment
idTips.description: Firmly attached to hard surfaces by a small, disc-like holdfast that grips tightly to rock surfaces in the intertidal zone

habitat: This seaweed grows in the rocky intertidal zone along New England's coast, typically attached to hard surfaces like granite ledges and boulder fields. It prefers areas with good water circulation and can tolerate both submersion at high tide and exposure to air at low tide. Look for it in tide pools and on wave-exposed rocky shores from the mid-intertidal zone down to shallow subtidal areas.

seasonality.spring: Fronds begin new growth and may appear brighter red as water temperatures start to warm. This is often the best time to spot fresh, undamaged specimens.
seasonality.summer: Mature fronds reach peak size and thickness. The distinctive truncated tips are most obvious during summer months when growth is most active.
seasonality.fall: Fronds may start to show wear from summer storms but remain identifiable. Color may deepen to darker red-purple hues as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Plants persist through winter but may appear smaller or more weathered. Storm damage is common, but the characteristic blunt-ended fronds remain recognizable on surviving specimens.

funFact: Despite being called a plant by many beachcombers, this "seaweed" is actually more closely related to the microscopic organisms that cause red tide blooms than it is to any land plant - it belongs to an entirely different kingdom of life that evolved in the ocean billions of years ago!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species might be confused with other red seaweeds like dulse or Irish moss, but the distinctive blunt, truncated frond tips set it apart - remember "truncated like it was trimmed with garden shears" to distinguish it from the pointed or rounded tips of other red seaweeds.
contextualKnowledge: The term "seaweed" is actually a bit of a misnomer since these marine algae aren't weeds at all, but rather important primary producers in ocean ecosystems. Many people don't realize that red, brown, and green "seaweeds" represent three completely different evolutionary lineages that are as distantly related to each other as they are to land plants.
compareHints: Since Coccotylus truncatus appears to be the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it with other members of the red seaweed family Phyllophoraceae by looking for the signature blunt-ended fronds. Other red seaweeds in New England typically have pointed, rounded, or branched tips, while this species maintains its distinctive "cut-off" appearance that gives it its scientific name.
